results.content: 2 Communication Complexity There are two parties are communicating, Alice and Bob, and they want to work together to compute the solution to some problem. The communication complexity of a problem is the minimum number of bits that Alice and Bob need to exchange to compute a solution in the worst case. There exists a way to partition any query problem (meaning that we give some of the inputs to Alice, and some to Bob) such that the communication complexity of the problem is at least the query complexity. To recap the above theorem, we can take any query problem—we don’t care at all about what it looks like—and there is a blackbox way of partitioning the inputs so that the same lower bounds hold in the communication complexity model of the problem, which is a much easier model.

# Communication Complexity of Cake Cutting. title={Communication Complexity of Cake Cutting},. Communication Complexity (opens in a new tab)Perfect Allocation (opens in a new tab)Cake-cutting Problems (opens in a new tab)Cake Cutting (opens in a new tab)Fair Allocation Problem (opens in a new tab)Moving Knives (opens in a new tab). ### The Query Complexity of Cake Cutting. Lower and upper bounds for computing approximately envy-free, perfect, and equitable allocations with the minimum number of cuts are given and a large subclass of this family, which captures all the known moving knife procedures, is formalized. NP-hardness results for various decision problems on the existence of envy-free allocations are established and connections between approximate and exact envy-freeness, as well as between continuous and discrete cake cutting are investigated. It is PPAD-complete to find an allocation -even using any constant number of possibly disconnected pieces- that makes just three agents envy-free, and this result has an interesting application for the envy-free cake cutting from fair division. ### Envy-Free Cake-Cutting for Four Agents. This work provides the first an Ω(n log n) lower bound on the complexity of any deterministic protocol in the standard model and introduces a version of cake cutting in which the players are able to cut with only finite precision. ### On the complexity of cake cutting. It is proved that in a certain, natural cake cutting model, every fair cake division protocol for n players must use @W(nlogn) cuts and evaluation queries in the worst case. It is shown that any deterministic strategy-proof protocol for two agents in the standard Robertson-Webb query model is dictatorial, that is, there is a fixed agent to which the protocol allocates the entire cake, and randomized protocols are exhibited that are truthful in expectation and compute approximately fair allocations. ### A Discrete and Bounded Envy-Free Cake Cutting Protocol for Any Number of Agents. This work considers the well-studied cake cutting problem and proposes a discrete and bounded envy-free protocol for any number of agents that can find in at most nn+1 queries an envy- free partial allocation of the cake. It is shown that the envy-free cake-cutting problem has the same complexity as finding a Brouwer's fixed point, or, more formally, it is PPAD-complete.
